# Write a Resume From Scratch (Even With No Work Experience)

> **In short:** A resume is a one-page story of what you've done, what you're good at, and what you want next — and you can build one from school, volunteering, caregiving, side jobs or hobbies. You don't need formal work experience; you need to describe your real life in the language employers recognize.

Writing a resume from zero feels harder than it is. Most "first resumes" stay blank because people think they have nothing to put on them. In reality, you've already handled deadlines, solved problems, dealt with people, and learned new things — you just haven't framed that work as work yet. This guide walks you through turning everyday experience into a clean, honest resume a hiring manager can read in under a minute.

## Before you start
- **A computer or phone** with a notes app, Google Docs, Microsoft Word, or a free resume builder (look for one by searching "free resume template").
- **About 60–90 minutes** for your first draft. After that, updates take 10 minutes.
- **A list of what you've actually done** — school, classes, projects, babysitting, family jobs, club roles, volunteering, online courses, certifications. Don't filter yet; just dump everything.
- **A job (or two) you'd like to apply to.** Even a saved job posting helps you match words later.

## Step 1 — Pick a clean, one-page layout
Open Google Docs and click **Template Gallery** in the top-right, or search for "resume" in Microsoft Word's template search. Pick something simple: name at the top, contact line below it, then clear section headings (think "section headers" — the bold labels that divide your resume into parts like Experience and Education). Avoid heavy designs, photos, or color blocks; hiring managers scan, they don't admire.

If templates feel overwhelming, just open a blank document and type your name big at the top. You'll add structure next. If you don't have Word or Docs, free builders like the ones from job search sites work too — search "free resume builder" and pick one with no signup wall.

💬 Example: section headers to copy — `Summary`, `Experience`, `Education`, `Skills`, `Projects`.

You'll know it worked when you have a blank one-page document with your name at the top and five empty sections waiting for content.

## Step 2 — Write a 2-sentence summary at the top
Under your name and contact info, add a **summary** — two short sentences that say who you are and what you're aiming for. Think of it as the cover of a book: it tells the reader what to expect inside. Use plain words, not job titles you haven't earned.

If you've never had a job, your summary can lean on what you're studying, what kind of work you want, and one strength. Keep it specific — "hardworking" doesn't say much, but "organized, comfortable with spreadsheets, and quick to learn new tools" paints a picture. If you don't know exactly what you want yet, write a **target** instead: "Looking for an entry-level role in retail, admin, or customer service."

💬 Example: "High school senior finishing in May 2026. Strong with customers, cash handling, and staying calm under pressure. Looking for part-time retail or front-desk work."

You'll know it worked when someone reading just those two sentences could guess what kind of job you'd be good at.

## Step 3 — Turn life experience into an "Experience" section
Create an **Experience** section heading and list anything where you showed up, did something, and someone (even a family member or teacher) noticed. Jobs count, but so do babysitting siblings, helping at a family store, school projects, volunteering at a food bank, mowing lawns, Discord servers you moderate, or a class group you led. For each entry, use this format: **Title — Where — Dates** (even if dates are approximate), then 2–4 short **bullet points** underneath describing what you did.

Each bullet should follow a simple recipe: *did what, using what skill, with what result.* You don't need fancy words; you need honest ones. If you watched three younger cousins every afternoon while your parent worked, that's "supervised and cared for three children daily, planned meals, handled minor conflicts, and maintained a consistent routine." That's a real bullet.

💬 Example (babysitting): `Cared for three children (ages 4–9) after school each day. Prepared snacks, helped with homework, and organized weekly craft activities.`

💬 Example (school project): `Led a 4-person team on a science fair project. Researched topics, delegated tasks, and presented findings to a panel of 5 judges.`

You'll know it worked when your experience list has 3–6 entries and every bullet describes something you actually did.

## Step 4 — Build an "Education" section and a "Skills" list
Add an **Education** section right below Experience. Include your school (or "Self-taught" / "Online coursework"), graduation year (or expected year), and one line of relevant classes or achievements — anything that hints at what you know. No degree yet? No problem: list what you ARE studying, plus any courses, workshops, or certificates, even free ones from sites like Coursera, Khan Academy, or YouTube tutorials.

Then add a **Skills** section. This is just a comma-separated list of tools and abilities: typing speed ("60+ WPM" if true — WPM means words per minute), languages, software (Google Sheets, Canva, TikTok editing, whatever you actually use), and people-skills ("customer service," "calm under pressure"). Skip anything you can't honestly do.

💬 Example education entry: `Lincoln High School — Expected graduation May 2027. Coursework: Business Math, Intro to Computer Science, Spanish II.`

💬 Example skills line: `Skills: Google Docs, Sheets, Canva, social media scheduling (Meta Business Suite), conversational Spanish, POS cash handling.`

You'll know it worked when a stranger could scan these two sections and quickly see what you know and where you learned it.

## Step 5 — Add optional sections that strengthen your story
Two more sections often help first-time resumes: **Projects** and **Volunteering**. A project can be anything you built or organized — a class group, a club, a YouTube channel, a small Etsy shop, a Discord community, a coding exercise. Volunteering covers anything you did for free that helped people — church groups, school events, neighborhood cleanups, food drives, coaching a kid's team.

You can also add **Languages**, **Certifications** (CPR, food handler's permit, even a free online certificate you actually finished), or **Awards** (perfect attendance, honor roll, employee-of-the-month at a family business — yes, that counts). If you have nothing extra, skip these — a tight two-page-equivalent on one page beats a sparse two pages.

💬 Example project entry: `Project: Neighborhood plant-swap app — designed a simple scheduling tool in Google Sheets, promoted via local Facebook group, coordinated 3 successful swaps with 40+ attendees.`

You'll know it worked when your resume fills the page naturally and every line answers "what did this person actually do?"

## Step 6 — Proofread, shorten, and save as a PDF
Read your resume out loud once. Fix anything that sounds awkward, too long, or that you can't defend in an interview. Most first drafts are too long; aim for one page. Cut filler like "hardworking team player" unless you back it up with an example. Replace vague verbs ("helped," "worked on") with specific ones ("organized," "built," "answered," "tracked," "taught").

Save the final file as a **PDF** (in Google Docs: **File → Download → PDF**; in Word: **File → Save As → PDF**). PDFs keep your formatting intact no matter who opens them. Name the file clearly: `FirstName-LastName-Resume.pdf`.

💬 Example: cut this — "Responsible for various tasks including helping customers." Replace with — "Greeted 80+ customers daily, restocked shelves, and handled returns at a family-run grocery store."

You'll know it worked when you can email the file, the formatting holds, and you feel ready to explain any line on it out loud.

## Common mistakes
- **Mistake:** Leaving the page half-empty because you think you "don't have experience." **Fix:** List school projects, caregiving, volunteering, hobbies done seriously, or small paid gigs — anything with responsibility counts. If the page is still sparse, add a one-line "Interests" section (photography, gaming communities, language learning) and tie one to a skill.
- **Mistake:** Using only generic words like "hardworking" and "team player." **Fix:** Replace each with a concrete example — "trained two new volunteers on check-in procedures" beats "good trainer" every time.
- **Mistake:** Lying or stretching the truth. **Fix:** Stick to what really happened, then frame it precisely. A hiring manager will ask follow-ups; honest, well-described experience always beats padded claims.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A resume is just a written summary of your life so far — once you've made one, updates for the next 10 years take minutes, not hours.
- **For your business or work:** If you hire people, a resume built this way tells you whether someone can actually describe what they did — a skill that predicts on-the-job clarity.
- **If you're just getting started:** Your first resume won't be perfect, and that's fine. Send it to one job you actually want, see what feedback comes back, and revise. Resume-writing is a skill, and it improves with each round.

## Try it now
Open a blank document right now and type your name at the top. Underneath, write one sentence describing what you're good at, and one sentence describing the kind of work you'd like. That's your summary. You just started a real resume — the rest is filling it in, one honest line at a time.
